source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Blind expert review found LLM ideas rated more novel than expert ideas, with no gain in feasibility. This is the main test of preliminary appraisal of ideas by judges.
numbers: 49 experts wrote ideas and 79 reviewed (104 people total). 298 unique reviews. Per-review test (109 reviews per condition): novelty human 4.84 vs AI 5.64 (p<0.01) vs AI plus human rerank 5.81. Per-idea test (N=49): 4.86 vs 5.62 vs 5.78 (p<0.05).
limits: Only 7 NLP topics, one prompt style, ideas not executed. Reviewers spent about 32 minutes per review. Novelty is a judgment, not a measured outcome.
agent_relevance: Novelty ratings by judges are a weak signal for the pursuit gate. See b05 and b06 for what happened once ideas were run.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: On the other metrics AI ideas matched human ideas. Feasibility was slightly lower for AI ideas, not significantly.
numbers: Per-idea means (N=49): feasibility human 6.53, AI 6.30, AI plus rerank 6.41. Excitement human 4.56, AI 5.18 (p=0.08), AI plus rerank 5.45 (p<0.01). Expected effectiveness human 5.10, AI 5.48, rerank 5.57 (not significant).
limits: Bonferroni-corrected Welch tests. The per-review table is less conservative than the idea-level test.
agent_relevance: The AI edge is in novelty and excitement only. Novelty alone must not drive the pursuit decision.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Reviewers agree only weakly on which ideas are best. LLM judges agree even less with the human consensus and sit near chance.
numbers: Human split-half agreement 56.1% (balanced accuracy, top vs bottom 25%). ICLR 2024 reviews on the same measure: 71.9%. GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%, Claude-3.5 pairwise 53.3%, AI Scientist reviewer 43.3%.
limits: Ground truth is human review scores, not executed outcomes. Low human agreement caps what any judge can score.
agent_relevance: Do not use a model judge as the pursuit selector. This supports guardrail G8: run it, do not opine on it.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: LLM idea generation runs out of diversity when scaled.
numbers: 4000 seed ideas generated per topic. Only about 5% (around 200) were non-duplicates at cosine similarity 0.8. The share of new non-duplicates fell as more ideas were generated, and the accumulated count plateaued.
limits: Duplicate threshold 0.8 chosen by manual inspection. One generator and one embedding model.
agent_relevance: Generating many ideas then picking one has a diversity ceiling. More samples do not widen the set of candidate directions for pursuit.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Executing the ideas reverses much of the AI idea advantage. This is the key test that separates appraisal from outcome.
numbers: 43 expert executors (19 human ideas, 24 AI ideas), 58 reviewers. Score change after execution on a 1-10 scale: human ideas novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; AI ideas fell by 1.049 (novelty), 1.760 (excitement), 1.879 (effectiveness). The difference in drops was significant on all four metrics (FDR-adjusted, p<0.05).
limits: Small N=43 projects. Post-execution rankings flipped (excitement AI 3.90 vs human 4.48; effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78) but the flip was not significant at idea level.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence that appraisal before running overrates fluent novel ideas. The pursuit gate should require a cheap execution probe before committing budget.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Pre-execution scores barely predict execution scores. For AI ideas, excitement even correlates negatively.
numbers: Ideation-to-execution correlation weak in most metrics; moderately negative for AI-idea excitement (Appendix D). Before execution AI ideas scored significantly higher on all four metrics.
limits: Correlation reported in an appendix. Small sample, so intervals are wide.
agent_relevance: A preliminary-appraisal score is a poor predictor of pursuit payoff. Treat it as a prior and update on a probe.

source: Wen, Si, Yueh-Han, He, Feng (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Benchmark for predicting which of two research ideas works better. Off-the-shelf frontier models are at chance. A fine-tuned model with retrieval is well above chance.
numbers: 1,585 test pairs (after model cut-off), 6,000 training pairs. Zero-shot GPT-4.1 51.9%; o1 and o3 similar or slightly better. Fine-tuned GPT-4.1 plus paper retrieval 77% on the full test set.
limits: Needs fine-tuning on thousands of past pairs. AI-research ideas only. Pairs come from published papers, so survivorship bias in what got published.
agent_relevance: Prompting alone cannot do the pursuit gate. A scaffold that only asks the model which idea is better should expect chance accuracy.

source: Wen, Si, Yueh-Han, He, Feng (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Expert humans are also poor at predicting idea outcomes. The fine-tuned system beat them on an NLP subset.
numbers: 25 experts, 45 idea pairs, 222 valid annotations. Majority vote of five experts 48.9%. Best-annotator-per-topic ceiling 60.0%. System 64.4%. Inter-annotator agreement 75.1% (NeurIPS 2021 reviewers 75.8%).
limits: Small human sample. The ceiling baseline was picked on the test set itself, so it is optimistic for humans.
agent_relevance: Human and model intuition for pursuit are both near chance. Annotators agree with each other but are not accurate, so agreement is not proof (supports G4).

source: Wen, Si, Yueh-Han, He, Feng (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: The system holds up on unpublished ideas from an AI ideation agent, but accuracy drops. Robustness tests checked for shortcuts such as idea complexity.
numbers: 63.6% accuracy on unpublished novel ideas (small-scale experiment with real ground truth). On pairs where the mathematically complex idea is worse, humans were misled and the model was not.
limits: Unpublished set is small. Accuracy falls from 77% to 63.6% out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Appraisal models degrade on new ideas. Expect lower accuracy for an agent's own fresh ideas than benchmark numbers.

source: Beel, Kan, Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist for Autonomous Research
finding: Independent evaluation of the AI Scientist found its built-in novelty check unreliable and its experiments often failing.
numbers: All 10 generated ideas and 2 seed ideas labelled novel, including well-known micro-batching for SGD. 5 of 12 experiments (42%) failed from coding errors. Code edits added only about 8% characters per iteration. Median 5 citations per paper; 5 of 34 citations from 2020 or later. Cost $6-$15 per paper, 3.5 hours human time.
limits: One group, one recommender-systems domain, run by a third-year CS student, earlier model versions. Authors call the setup time a lower bound.
agent_relevance: Keyword-search novelty gates over-accept. A pursuit gate that asks 'is it novel' via search will pass known ideas.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: An automated paper reviewer used as an appraisal judge is only human-level.
numbers: GPT-4o reviewer with 5 self-reflection rounds, 5 ensembled reviews and a 1-shot example: 70% accuracy vs 73% for humans in the NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment. F1 0.57 vs 0.49 for humans; AUC 0.65 for both, at threshold score 6.
limits: Authors' own evaluation. Reviews finished papers, not early ideas. Authors report hallucinated plots and tables in generated papers.
agent_relevance: Even a tuned model judge only matches a noisy human consensus. Use it as one signal at most.

source: Yamada et al. (2025) The AI Scientist-v2: Workshop-Level Automated Scientific Discovery via Agentic Tree Search
finding: Tree search over experiment nodes, chosen by a scalar score, produced one workshop-acceptable paper out of three.
numbers: 3 fully autonomous manuscripts submitted to an ICLR workshop. One scored 6.33 average (top 45%) and would have passed meta-review; it reported a negative result. It was withdrawn after acceptance, by prior agreement.
limits: N=3 papers. Workshop bar is low. Authors say it lacks main-conference rigor and had inaccuracies. Reviewers could opt out of AI papers.
agent_relevance: Best-first selection of which branch to pursue by a real measured score is a workable pursuit rule.

source: Li et al. (2024) Chain of Ideas: Revolutionizing Research via Novel Idea Development with LLM Agents
finding: Organising literature as a chain of developing ideas improves generated ideas. Developmental trend matters more than volume of related papers.
numbers: Idea Arena pairwise evaluation. CoI agent ranked first among automated baselines, 56 ELO above the second best in human evaluation. Authors state ideas as novel as human experts.
limits: Authors' own benchmark and judges. LLM judging in the Arena carries bias risk (see b03).
agent_relevance: Giving the model the trajectory of the field is a form of Nickles-style discoverability: show how earlier ideas led to the next.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Scientific Discovery
finding: Nickles treats discovery methodology as generative justification: reasoning to a claim, judged by whether it could have been found with the available information.
numbers: Nickles 1984, 1985, 1989. Contrast: consequential justification (success on novel predictions). Laudan 1980 adds a third context, pursuit. Schaffner 1993 separates weak (promising) from strong (approximately true) evaluation.
limits: SEP reports no direct empirical test of generative justification, the pursuit context or weak evaluation. Support is from historical reconstruction.
agent_relevance: Weak vs strong evaluation maps to the S0 gate: a cheap promise check separate from final proof. No hard evidence exists, so test it in our own loop.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Scientific Discovery
finding: Darden's schema instantiation and heuristics are sufficient, not necessary, and only weakly normative.
numbers: Darden 1991, 2002, 2009: protein synthesis found by instantiating 'reactant1 + reactant2 = product'. Wimsatt 2007: heuristics bring systematic biases. Hey 2016 asks for principles to evaluate heuristics. Chow 2015: 'heuristic' has many meanings.
limits: Built from rational reconstructions of past cases, so case selection may bias the list.
agent_relevance: Schema instantiation can be an operator, but must be measured against plain prompting before it earns a place (G7).

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Social Epistemology
finding: Zollman effect: in models, more communication can lower group accuracy because misleading early evidence spreads and the group stops exploring too soon.
numbers: Zollman 2007, 2010 following Bala and Goyal 1998. Helpful: transient diversity, stubbornness (Frey and Seselja 2020), grant policy (Kummerfeld and Zollman 2020). Networks sensitive to evidence pick the better theory more often (Zollman 2013; Rosenstock et al. 2017).
limits: Abstract bandit models. Parameter sensitivity of the effect is not covered in the page text I read.
agent_relevance: Do not let samples see each other's answers early. Keep branches apart until a real check separates them (G4).

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Social Epistemology
finding: Weisberg and Muldoon's maverick result was criticised, then partly restored in modified models.
numbers: Weisberg and Muldoon 2009 found mixed followers and mavericks beat either alone. Alexander, Himmelreich, Thompson 2015, Thoma 2015, Poyhonen 2017 and Fernandez Pinto 2018 criticise it. Thoma 2015 and Poyhonen 2017 find the cognitive diversity benefit in modified versions.
limits: Model-dependent. No data from real labs.
agent_relevance: Mixing explorers and exploiters is plausible but model-dependent. Do not hard-code a ratio without our own measurement.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Social Epistemology
finding: Kitcher's division of labor: credit seekers spread over problems better than pure truth seekers, who herd. Zollman 2018 argues credit is not needed.
numbers: Kitcher 1990; Strevens 2003 (priority rule better); Zollman 2018 critique.
limits: Idealised agents. No empirical test cited.
agent_relevance: A budget rule should deliberately spread effort over several candidate ideas rather than put all on the current favorite.

source: Borg, Frey, Seselja, Strasser (2017) An argumentative agent-based model of scientific inquiry
finding: Agent-based model of rival theories: sharing information helped or did not hurt, which differs from the Zollman effect.
numbers: Theories are trees of depth 3, 4 children per node, attack probability 0.3. 100 runs per setting, 10-100 agents. Homogeneous groups with no sharing did worst. Heterogeneous groups with no sharing were much more successful than homogeneous ones. Biased agents did worse as information flow rose. Exact rates only in figures.
limits: Authors call it a 'bookshelf model'. Anomalies appear only as attacks from rival theories. Evaluation by defensibility, not heuristic promise.
agent_relevance: Whether sharing helps depends on the model. Starting agents on different theories is the safe default when evidence is absent.

source: Seselja and Strasser (2014) Epistemic justification in the context of pursuit: a coherentist approach
finding: Search snippet only: proposes coherence-based indicators of pursuitworthiness, namely potential consistency, potential inferential density, potential explanatory power.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Full text blocked (403).
agent_relevance: Candidate checklist for the pursuit gate; verify before use.

source: Alexander, Himmelreich, Thompson (2015) Epistemic landscapes, optimal search, and the division of cognitive labor, Philosophy of Science 82(3)
finding: Search snippet only: claims seeking novel approaches need not be optimal and doubts benefits of social learning in complex landscapes.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened. Full text blocked (403). Snippet says pure maverick populations vastly outperformed others in the 2009 original.
agent_relevance: Warns against assuming novelty-seeking is always the best search rule.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor
finding: Original model of followers and mavericks on an epistemic landscape. Known only through SEP and a search snippet.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened (403). See b17.
agent_relevance: Origin of the explorer-versus-exploiter argument.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Executors were randomly assigned ideas, which controls confounds.
numbers: 43 executors completed; 7 institutions; 6 AI ideas had human-proposed baselines altered during execution.
limits: Some executors dropped out before completion. Execution was limited in time and compute.
agent_relevance: Compare like with like when testing a pursuit rule: same budget for every candidate.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery
finding: AI Scientist v1 used a literature-search novelty check with a stop rule and a binary novel label. The other idea scores were not used downstream.
numbers: Up to 10 search rounds before the novelty decision; per Beel et al., interestingness, feasibility and novelty scores were not used in later processing.
limits: Beel et al. describe the pipeline from code and logs; mixed sources.
agent_relevance: Ratings that nothing reads are decoration. Every score the schema emits should drive a transition.

source: Wen, Si, Yueh-Han, He, Feng (2025) Predicting Empirical AI Research Outcomes with Language Models
finding: Chain-of-thought sampling did not help the fine-tuned predictor.
numbers: Neither sampled nor LM-selected reasoning chains improved over the baseline predictor.
limits: Authors only suspect a reason.
agent_relevance: Extra reasoning text before a pursuit choice may add cost without accuracy.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers
finding: Mixed-effects and per-reviewer tests agreed with the main novelty result, and the per-topic breakdown was underpowered.
numbers: Three tests: per review, per idea, per reviewer. Mixed-effects model (Table 17) supports the novelty effect. Per-topic samples small, so most topic-level results are not significant.
limits: Authors say per-topic results are only suggestive.
agent_relevance: Effects hold across analysis choices at the pooled level, not for each topic.
